title: I am someone else (2:4)
hook: the returner cries out, gives, keeps away from the cause, even changes name and deeds
tomorrow: is a private sorry enough when others heard the wrong?

segments.voice: Yesterday: let go first. Confession with the wrong still in your fist is immersing with a sheretz in hand. Today, what the open hand does next.
screen: `LET GO FIRST.` → `WHAT THE OPEN HAND DOES.`

segments.voice: You haven't changed a bit. At a reunion, it's a compliment. After a fight, it's a verdict. So can a person actually become someone else? Maimonides says yes, and he lists the ways. The returner cries out before God, with tears and pleading. Gives tzedakah, as much as they're able. Keeps far away from the thing that tripped them. And then two surprises: they change their deeds, all of them, toward the good, and they may even change their name.
screen: `YOU HAVEN'T CHANGED A BIT.` → `CRY OUT, GIVE, KEEP AWAY.` → `A NEW NAME.`

segments.voice: Why a name? Maimonides gives the returner's own words: as if to say, I am someone else, not the one who did those things. He even adds leaving home for a while, exile, as part of the turn. Here's the best case for this view: change needs room. A new name, a new street, new habits give the new person somewhere to stand, so the old one isn't waiting on every corner. Now the other voice, from the Talmud. Reish Lakish says return is so great that deliberate sins become like merits, when the return comes from love. In a Talmud story, Reish Lakish himself had lived as a bandit before he turned to study. On this view, the past isn't shed like a coat. It becomes fuel. The one who did it is exactly the one who now knows better, and the history is put to work. Its best case: you can't help the next person climb out of a hole you pretend you were never in. So one voice says: I am someone else now. The other says: I'm the same person, and that's why this counts. Both are inside the tradition, and both agree on one thing. The proof is the deeds.
screen: `NOT THE ONE WHO DID THOSE THINGS.` · `CHANGE NEEDS ROOM.` · `SINS BECOME MERITS.` · `THE PROOF IS THE DEEDS.` · then, large: `I AM SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you'd like to be different about you this week. Name the wish, then the one obstacle most likely to get in its way. Then make a plan in a single sentence, if this happens, then I'll do that, and rest with it until the bell.
I am someone else: the returner's words in Maimonides, not the one who did those things. Said with new deeds, and sometimes a new name.
Carry this one: I am someone else now, or, if you lean the other way, the same someone, turned. Day fifteen forty-three.

screen: `DAY 1543 COUNTS.` → `MAIMONIDES, THE LAWS OF RETURN · 6 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: IS A PRIVATE SORRY ENOUGH WHEN OTHERS HEARD THE WRONG?`

howItsDone: Some Jews study these ways of return in the days before Yom Kippur, when giving tzedakah and asking people for forgiveness are part of the season for some families.

fork.setup: your friend Owen says changing your name after doing wrong is just running from it. what's Maimonides' best case back?
options: a new name gives new deeds room: I am someone else, not the one who did it.
a new name hides the past, so nobody can ever hold it against you.
a new name is the whole of return; once it's changed, the rest follows.
fork.reveal: Maimonides pairs the name with changed deeds. and Owen's worry has a voice inside the tradition too: Reish Lakish keeps the past and puts it to work.

what a scholar hears: Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:4 (a changed name, changed deeds, exile) beside Reish Lakish in Yoma 86b, where sins become merits.

chat.says: mom: 'you always say sorry, then do it again.' can people actually become someone else?
options: Maimonides says yes: one changed deed, then more, till you're not who did it.
Not really; people are who they are, so say sorry more often and move on.
Only with a big move, like a new name or leaving town; small stuff can't.
chat.meaning: Maimonides lists ways of return and ends on changed deeds. A name or a move can help, but the deeds are the proof.

tzedakah.meaning: giving to those in need; also righteousness, justice

Reish Lakish.meaning: a Talmud sage who said sins can become merits

Talmud.meaning: the collection of rabbinic discussion and law

Maimonides.meaning: medieval rabbi and philosopher; wrote the Laws of Return

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:4 (crying out, charity, keeping away, a changed name, changed deeds, exile)
Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 86b (Reish Lakish: return from love turns deliberate sins into merits)
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 84a (Reish Lakish's life before study)

notes: Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:4 paraphrased; 'as if to say, I am someone else, not the one who did those things' renders 'ani acher, ve'eini oto ha'ish she'asah otam hama'asim'. Confirm.

Yoma 86b: Reish Lakish's two sayings (from fear, sins become like errors; from love, like merits); only the love clause is used. Confirm framing as a second view rather than a contradiction of Maimonides.
Bava Metzia 84a: Reish Lakish described as a bandit (listim) before study; some render it gladiator. Confirm wording.
Debate day: two views (a clean break vs. the past put to work), each given its best case; practice kind: a plan (wish, obstacle, plan).
